situation: My dog Rufus died last Tuesday and the house is too quiet without his collar jingling in the hall.
poem:
The hall keeps the shape of a small bright jingle,
and Rufus is the silence wearing his collar.
Dusk pours its slow grey through the empty doorway,
and every board remembers the weight of him.

situation: The letter came today: I have been accepted to the marine biology program in Bergen.
poem:
The letter opens like a door onto salt water,
and Bergen glitters, cold and blue, and calls.
O the deep green rooms you will go learning,
the whole ringing ocean saying your name aloud.

situation: My mother's biopsy results come back on Friday and I have cleaned the kitchen three times.
poem:
You have scoured the kitchen to a pale shine,
three times, and Friday will not come faster.
The faucet drips its small bright coin of sound.
Waiting is a held breath with no shore.

situation: I have been waiting at the DMV in chair forty-two for two hours and my number still has not been called.
poem:
Chair forty-two has learned the shape of you,
and the clock drips like cold amber, slow.
Numbers rise and are not yours, not yours.
O grey room, O long unhurried afternoon.

situation: My landlord kept my whole deposit for one scuff on the baseboard and will not answer his phone.
poem:
One scuff on the baseboard, and he keeps it all,
your money swallowed by a silent ringing phone.
The red rises in your throat, and it is honest.
O landlord, may your baseboards never shine.

situation: The tornado passed two streets over and our oak tree is still standing.
poem:
Two streets over, the sky went black and roaring,
and here our oak still holds its thousand hands.
The air comes back, green-washed and strangely sweet.
We are still here. The leaves are still here.

situation: I burned the first pancake again, the way my grandmother always did, and the smoke alarm went off.
poem:
The first pancake blackens, as it always must,
and your grandmother laughs somewhere in the smoke.
The alarm sings its small shrill hymn above you,
and the second one comes out gold.

situation: My daughter Maya took her first steps across the kitchen tile this morning, straight into the dog's water bowl.
poem:
Maya goes swaying out across the kitchen tile,
four steps, then the bright astonished splash.
The water bowl receives her like a small sea,
and the whole room laughs its yellow laugh.

situation: I sold my father's blue Volvo yesterday and forgot to take the pine air freshener off the mirror.
poem:
The blue car goes down the road without you,
and the pine still turning on its little string.
Your father's hands are somewhere in that wheel,
driving off through the long amber evening.

situation: I have to give a toast at my brother's wedding on Saturday and I have rewritten it eleven times.
poem:
Eleven drafts, and still the words go crooked,
and Saturday comes walking up the aisle.
Your brother will not hear the eleven; he'll hear you.
The glass will shake a little. That is love.

situation: It has rained for six days and I have reread the same page of my library book four times.
poem:
Six days of rain, and the page will not turn.
The same grey sentence, the same drowned light.
The library book sleeps open on your knee.
Outside, the gutters keep their one long note.

situation: Someone keyed my car in the grocery store lot while I was inside buying milk.
poem:
You went in for milk; you came out scarred,
a long white wound down the door's blue flank.
Someone's hand did that, quick and cowardly,
and the cart wheels rattle like small teeth.

situation: My flight from Denver landed twenty minutes before the blizzard closed the runway. I have never been so glad to see a jetway.
poem:
Twenty minutes, and the runway shut its white mouth,
and you already down, and warm, and breathing.
Denver goes under, a slow drowning of lights,
and your hands unclench, one finger at a time.

situation: I found a five dollar bill in my winter coat pocket along with a movie ticket from last February.
poem:
A folded five and a February ticket stub,
both wintering in the dark of your pocket.
Small gold, small ghost of a Tuesday film,
the coat gives back what the coat kept.

situation: My best friend Priya moved to Auckland on Sunday and we finished the last of the chili in her freezer.
poem:
The last of the chili, eaten standing up,
and Priya already somewhere over the Pacific.
Auckland will have her mornings now, and her laugh,
and the freezer hums its cold blue nothing.

situation: After eleven months of looking, I start the new job at the bakery on Monday.
poem:
Eleven months of doors, and now this one opens,
and it smells of yeast and warm brown crust.
Monday comes up golden as a risen loaf,
and your hands have somewhere to be.

situation: My son has not texted back in three days and his last message was just a period.
poem:
Three days, and that small black period holding,
a door pulled almost shut, a held stone.
You watch the screen the way you watched his crib.
The silence has a weight. You carry it.

situation: I finally fixed the squeaking gate with a bit of olive oil because I could not find the WD-40.
poem:
A spoon of olive oil, and the gate forgives,
its long complaint gone soft as green fruit.
Now it swings on a hinge of small mercy,
and the yard is quieter by one voice.

situation: My coworker Dan presented my spreadsheet in the Tuesday meeting and never once said my name.
poem:
Dan stood and read your columns like his own,
and your name stayed folded in his pocket.
The room nodded at the wrong bright face,
and the numbers, yours, went on without you.

situation: The cat came back after four nights out, thin and loud, and slept twelve hours on my sweater.
poem:
Four nights of open window and no cat,
and now this thin loud hunger at the door.
He sleeps a whole clock through on your sweater,
and the house sets its heart down again.
